questions.q: A user holds the `hr_admin` role. The field-level ACL on `employee.salary_band` only grants access to members of an `hr_compensation` group or holders of `hr_compensation_admin`. Can this user read the field?
options: Yes, because hr_admin implies every other HR-related role automatically
No -- field-level security only checks the specific exception list this field was scoped to, regardless of what other roles the user holds
Yes, because field-level ACLs never apply to users with any admin-sounding role
It depends on whether the user also passes the table-level ACL, with no field-level check needed
questions.explain: Deny by default, allow by exception means only the explicitly listed group/role passes -- unrelated roles, even administrative ones, don't grant an automatic exception.

questions.q:
Read this field ACL script:
```javascript
answer = gs.getUser().isMemberOf('b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7') ||
  gs.hasRole('hr_compensation_admin');
```
What design pattern does this script follow?
options: Allow by default, deny by exception
Deny by default, allow by exception -- access is denied unless the user matches one of two narrow, explicit checks
It grants access to any authenticated user
It denies access to everyone, with no possible exception
questions.explain: The script returns true only for a specific group or a specific role -- everyone else is denied by default.

questions.q: What is the real relationship between a field-level ACL and Data Anonymization on the same sensitive field?
options: They do the same job, so only one is ever needed
A field-level ACL decides whether a user can see the field at all; anonymization, as a second layer, can mask how much of the value is revealed to those who pass -- defense in depth
Anonymization replaces the need for any ACL on that field
A field-level ACL can only be applied after anonymization is configured
questions.explain: They're independent layers: the ACL is a binary gate, anonymization controls how much of the visible value is actually shown.

questions.q: What real-world problem does over-restricting a field tend to cause?
options: It has no real downside -- more restriction is always safer
It legitimately blocks people who need the data to do their job, leading to constant escalations or workarounds
It automatically triggers a security audit
It makes the field-level ACL run faster
questions.explain: Over-restricting breaks real workflows -- the honest tradeoff this lesson emphasizes, not a one-sided case for maximum restriction.

questions.q: What does a well-designed field-level security setup actually look like, per this lesson?
options: Every sensitive-looking field locked down to the admin role only
No field-level ACLs at all, relying solely on table-level security
The real, specific minimum access each role genuinely needs for that field, worked out deliberately rather than defaulting to either extreme
Every field anonymized regardless of sensitivity
questions.explain: The lesson's honest tradeoff: neither blanket lock-down nor blanket openness is good design -- the goal is the genuine minimum access each role needs.
